topic: Identifying SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS and HL evidence

problems.desc: all three pairs of sides carry matching tick marks, so the criterion is SSS. The three congruence statements are that the first side of one triangle is congruent to the corresponding side of the other, and likewise for the second and third pairs; a correct response names all three pairs using the vertex letters shown, in corresponding order.

part (a): the missing piece for SAS is a pair of congruent angles, and it must be the angle formed where the two already-marked sides meet in each triangle -- the included angle. An angle anywhere else gives side-side-angle, which proves nothing.
part (b): for SSS the missing piece is the third pair of sides, that is the remaining side of each triangle marked congruent to the other; no angle information is needed at all.

part (a): the criterion is HL, since both triangles are right triangles and the matching parts are a hypotenuse and a leg. A correct response also says why the same pattern fails in general: in a triangle that is not right, two sides and a non-included angle can be arranged in two different ways, so the two triangles need not be congruent. The right angle removes that second arrangement.

part (a): the property is the reflexive property of congruence -- any segment is congruent to itself -- so the shared diagonal may be written as a congruent pair even though no tick mark shows it. It is legitimate because the two triangles genuinely contain the same segment, and the property is an axiom of congruence rather than something that needs proving.
part (b): with the shared side added, the marked side, the marked angle between it and the shared side, and the shared side give SAS.

part (a): the unmarked pair is the pair of angles at the crossing point, which are vertical angles and therefore congruent by the vertical angles theorem. With the marked angle pair, the marked side pair and that vertical pair, the side lies opposite one of the two angles rather than between them, so the criterion is AAS.

part (b): a correct response explains that two sides and an angle not between them do not fix a triangle -- the second side can swing to two different positions, producing two non-congruent triangles from the same three measurements -- so side-side-angle is not a congruence criterion and the classmate's argument establishes nothing.
